title: Observability
goal: You cannot operate what you cannot see. Do this before the optional deep end — those steps are far harder to debug blind.
startWith: Several services exchanging events. The more of them there are, the more this pays.

newIdeas.plain: A trace is one user request's whole journey. A span is one unit of work inside it — an HTTP call, a database query, a message being consumed. Spans nest, so a trace is a tree you can read top to bottom.

Passing the trace id from one service to the next, so their spans join the same trace. Over HTTP it is a header and Spring does it for you. Over Kafka it is a message header, and it only works if you enable observation on both the template and the listener — miss one and every trace stops at the broker.

Metrics: numbers over time, cheap, tell you something is wrong. Traces: one request in detail, tell you where. Logs: the specifics, tell you what. You want all three sharing a trace id so you can move between them.

OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard. Micrometer is Spring's instrumentation API, which exports to it. The grafana/otel-lgtm image bundles Loki, Grafana, Tempo and Prometheus in one container so you can have all three signals locally without operating four services.
Recording every trace is affordable locally and not in production. Sample at 1.0 here, 1-10% there, and always sample errors.

tasks.do: Run the Grafana LGTM stack and export from every service
tasks.why: One container gives you traces, metrics and logs with somewhere to look at them.
tasks.how: Add the dependencies to each service and one shared configuration block. The two Kafka observation lines are the ones that matter most in this project — without them your traces stop dead at the broker and the interesting half of the story is missing.

blocks.label: Add the LGTM container
blocks.body:
cat >> infra/compose/docker-compose.yml << 'EOF'

  lgtm:
    image: grafana/otel-lgtm:latest
    container_name: lf-lgtm
    ports: ["3000:3000", "4317:4317", "4318:4318"]
EOF
docker compose -f infra/compose/docker-compose.yml up -d lgtm

blocks.label: Shared config — the Kafka lines carry traces across the hop
blocks.body:
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0          # 1.0 locally, 0.01-0.1 in production
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://localhost:4318/v1/traces
spring:
  kafka:
    template:
      observation-enabled: true   # <- without these two, traces
    listener:
      observation-enabled: true   #    stop at the broker

blocks.label: Open Grafana (admin / admin)
blocks.body:
start http://localhost:3000      # Windows
# macOS: open http://localhost:3000

check.expect: HTTP metrics are registered, and traces appear in Grafana's Tempo view.

tasks.do: Verify one trace spans the whole workflow
tasks.why: This is the acceptance test for the whole step: one id, six services, one readable tree.
tasks.how: Place a payment and find its trace in Grafana. You should be able to follow payment → Kafka → ledger → Kafka → payment without losing the thread. If it breaks at a particular hop, that hop is missing observation configuration.

blocks.label: Place a payment, then find its trace
blocks.body:
curl -s -X POST localhost:8085/api/v1/payments -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"accountId":"11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111","wallets":["A-15"],"amount":4500}' | jq
# then in Grafana: Explore -> Tempo -> search by service name

tasks.do: Add domain metrics and put ids on every log line
tasks.why: Framework metrics tell you the system is busy. Domain metrics tell you the business is broken.
tasks.how: ledgerflow.saga.compensated tagged by step and reason is worth more than any latency histogram: it is the number that tells you customers are being turned away. Put traceId, correlationId and paymentId in the MDC so a log search and a trace lead to each other.

tasks.do: Alert on consumer lag and dead letter depth
tasks.why: These two are your earliest warnings, and both are silent by default.
tasks.how: Rising lag means you cannot keep up. A DLT with anything in it means messages are being abandoned. Treat DLT depth above zero as an incident rather than a metric — a threshold of 'more than a few' is how backlogs go unnoticed for weeks.

blocks.label: Alert rules (sketch)
blocks.body:
kafka_consumer_fetch_manager_records_lag_max > 1000 for 5m   -> page
sum(dlt_topic_depth) > 0                                     -> page
ledgerflow_saga_compensated_total rate > baseline            -> investigate

proof.expect: Click a failed payment, read the whole story, jump to that request's logs.
proof.note: Dead letter depth above zero is an incident, not a metric. Alert on it accordingly.

doneWhen: One trace covers a whole payment across every service and both Kafka hops, and you can get from it to the matching logs.

lessons.title: Endpoints tool window
lessons.teach: Endpoints lists every mapping in every service, with the ability to call one. It is the fastest audit of "what does this system actually expose" when you start instrumenting.
lessons.fallbackTip: Ultimate only. Community: the actuator mappings endpoint.
